blocks.text: The hydrogen bond is a special type of dipole-dipole force. It is the strongest of the intermolecular forces but weaker than all the major types of bond, ionic, metallic and covalent. A hydrogen bond forms when two conditions are fulfilled: the hydrogen atom is connected to a highly electronegative atom such as F, O or N, and that electronegative atom has a lone pair of electrons. The covalent bond between a highly electronegative atom and hydrogen is highly polarized, so the hydrogen carries a sufficient delta+ charge and the electronegative atom a delta- charge; the lone pair on the electronegative atom lets the partially positive hydrogen make a bond with F, O or N, the hydrogen bond, shown by a dotted line, whose strength is about one tenth of an ordinary covalent bond. The number of hydrogen bonds a molecule can form on average depends on the number of hydrogen atoms bonded to the electronegative atom and the number of lone pairs on the F, O or N.

A water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and two lone pairs on oxygen, so it forms two hydrogen bonds on average; water molecules are therefore extensively hydrogen bonded, which gives water its characteristic properties, such as its high boiling point of 100 degrees C, and in the liquid the molecules are arranged three-dimensionally, the bonding bridging two electronegative oxygen atoms. Ammonia forms only one hydrogen bond per molecule despite three hydrogen atoms, because nitrogen has only one lone pair; its hydrogen bonding is much weaker than water's and its boiling point much lower, -33 degrees C. HF has three lone pairs on fluorine, which would allow three bonds, but only one hydrogen atom, so it too is restricted to one bond; yet the bond is strong because of fluorine's high electronegativity, and its boiling point (19.9 degrees C) is much higher than ammonia's (-33.5 degrees C). In the solid, HF molecules join in a zig-zag chain through hydrogen bonds. The exceptionally low acidic strength of HF compared with HCl, HBr and HI is attributed to this strong hydrogen bonding, because the partially positive hydrogen is trapped between two highly electronegative atoms.
